name: sequin
why: Turns raw ANSI escape sequences into human-readable text, a small window into how terminals actually talk.

brief.what_it_is: Sequin is a small command-line filter from Charm that takes raw text containing ANSI/VT escape sequences on stdin and prints a human-readable description of each sequence, so you can see what the escape codes are doing. It can also run a program for you in a fake TTY with `sequin -- <command>`, and its `-r`/`--raw` flag highlights sequences inline in the original text instead of describing them. The README describes it as "Human-readable ANSI sequences."
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is a utility for debugging CLIs and TUIs, for describing escape sequences you don't understand, and for exploring what TUIs do under the hood. It also mentions inspecting golden files from Bubble Tea's teatest.
brief.how_it_works: Sequin relies on the `ansi` package from Charm's `x` project (github.com/charmbracelet/x/ansi). While it walks through the input string, it pretty-prints what each sequence is and what it does. The FAQ also notes that some background-colour queries (OSC 10/11) go through to the terminal, so multiplexer version and config matter for those.

brief.install_notes: brew install sequin works on macOS and Linux. The README also lists AUR (yay -S sequin-bin), Nix (nix-shell -p sequin, and nur.repos.charmbracelet.sequin via NUR), a Debian/Ubuntu apt repo at repo.charm.sh (needs adding a signing key and sources.list entry), a Fedora/RHEL yum repo, and go install. Prebuilt binaries cover Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD, and Debian and RPM packages are on the releases page. Packaged installs ship shell completions for Bash, ZSH, Fish and PowerShell; from-source builds generate them with `sequin completion <shell> -h`. No accounts or runtime config are needed beyond a terminal and, for some multiplexer setups, TERM and COLORTERM settings.
brief.standout: Rather than just stripping escape codes, it names each sequence and explains its effect, which makes it a learning tool as well as a debugger. The `sequin -- <cmd>` fake-TTY mode and the `-r` inline-highlight mode mean you can inspect a program's real output without having to set up a terminal.
brief.status: quiet. The latest release is v0.3.1, dated 27 Jan 2025, with v0.3.0 on 9 Dec 2024 and v0.2.0 and earlier in Nov 2024. I did not check commit history or open issues, and the README has no maintenance note. Activity looks slower after January 2025, but the project was still being released at that point.
brief.caveats: The README says it is not finished: common sequences are implemented, but APC sequences are not supported yet. Many programs emit plain text when piped, so you may need to force colour (the README mentions CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 or a program's own ANSI flags). Inside tmux or GNU screen, background-colour queries only work with tmux 3.4 or later or screen 4.99.0 or later, plus the right default-terminal and COLORTERM settings. The FAQ also says `defbce on` is needed in screenrc to avoid background-colour differences. The project is MIT licensed.

entry.title: sequin
entry.tldr: Pipe any program's coloured output into sequin and it names every ANSI escape sequence and says what it does, a quick look at how terminals are told what to draw.
entry.deeper_look:
Sequin is a small filter from Charm. It reads text containing ANSI/VT escape sequences on stdin and prints a plain description of each one: which colour is being set, what is switched on or off, where the cursor moves. With `-r` it keeps the original text and highlights the sequences inline instead. With `sequin -- <command>` it runs the program for you in a fake TTY, so the program behaves as if it were talking to a real terminal.

The README pitches it as a debugging tool for CLIs and TUIs, for describing escape sequences you don't understand, and for exploring what TUIs do under the hood. It also mentions inspecting golden files generated by Bubble Tea's teatest.

The idea underneath is that a terminal is not a canvas. Everything a program does to it, from bold text to colour to cursor movement, travels as ordinary bytes in the same stream as the text, marked off by an escape character. Most people never see those bytes because the terminal swallows them. Sequin makes them visible and gives them names. It builds on the `ansi` package from Charm's `x` project, which is where the parsing lives.

It is a learning tool as much as a debugger. Run `ls` or `git status` through it and you see what your everyday tools say to your terminal all day.

try_this.what_happens: Sends a short string with colour, bold and reverse-video codes into sequin, which explains each sequence.
Shows the escape sequences git emits for its coloured status output, described one by one.

entry.whats_unique: It names each sequence and explains its effect rather than just stripping or dumping the bytes. The fake-TTY mode lets you inspect a program's real output without setting anything up.
entry.caveats: The README says it is unfinished: common sequences are covered but APC sequences are not yet supported, and many programs drop colour when piped unless you force it.
